result:
I've been thinking about the word "almost."

It's one of the few words that points at a thing by describing the space right next to it. "Almost round." "Almost finished." "Almost said something." The word doesn't name the thing; it names the gap. And the gap, it turns out, is where most of life happens.

Consider: nothing is actually round. Not a coin, not a planet, not the pupil of an eye. Roundness is a definition that lives in geometry books, and every physical object is some distance from it. But we don't experience the world as a collection of failures to be circular. We experience coins as round. "Almost" is doing quiet work everywhere, and we've agreed not to mention it.

I like that there's a whole grammar of proximity. Nearly, practically, virtually, just about, on the verge of, within a hair of. Each one measures a slightly different kind of distance. "Nearly" feels temporal—you were on your way. "Practically" feels like a shrug—close enough, who's counting. "On the verge" has a cliff in it. English speakers pick among these without thinking, and the choice reveals something about how the person sees the gap: as a delay, as a rounding error, as a precipice.

There's also the melancholy version. "Almost" is the word of near-misses, the train pulling away as you reach the platform, the sentence you had ready and didn't say. Those moments have a peculiar weight because they're so specific. A total miss is abstract—you were never in the running. But almost means you can see, in detail, the version where it went the other way. The gap is small enough to picture crossing.

And yet I don't think "almost" is fundamentally sad. Most of what we call skill is the management of almost. A musician plays almost in time, and the slight deviations are called feel. A translator finds the word that almost means the same thing, and the residue is where the two languages actually touch. A friend almost understands you, and the effort of closing that last distance is what makes it friendship rather than telepathy.

Maybe that's what I find appealing. "Almost" is honest about the fact that we never fully arrive, and generous about how much we can do from just outside the door. It's the word of asymptotes—approaching, forever approaching—but said in a tone that suggests approaching is a perfectly good way to spend a life.

Anyway. I almost wrote about something else.
